What the hell actually happens during a code review?

Typically, an engineer will submit a piece of code that they have just finished writing, and a few other engineers will read over the code, looking for things like:

  • logic bugs
  • security flaws
  • poor implementation
  • lack of comments
  • general readability and ease of understanding

If any problems are found, comments are left about how to fix them, and the original engineer makes the recommended changes, and then submits the code for review again.

Once the code passes review, it's accepted into the "master branch" of the software in question.

Yes, you can absolutely work in this field without a formal education! I don't actually have a college degree. I dropped out when I got my first decent job offer.

The trick is to find the first employer that will risk hiring you based purely on your display of skill and knowledge. You could also try to do some freelance stuff first, but I've never gone that route, so I can't speak to it much. Once you get some professional experience under your belt, and on your resume, the lack of formal education stops mattering as much. Some small subset of employers will still refuse to hire you, and others will encourage you to take classes after you're hired, but most just don't care, in my experience.

My advice is to pick one language and learn it really well. If I had to pick one to recommend, the easiest and most marketable right now is probably Java.

Try to create some useful software for yourself. Just identify a problem you have, no matter how small, and engineer a solution to it. Save all of the code you write (use a VCS, like Git).

A few things you should learn to do, other than writing great code, are:

  • document the code you write
  • make your code well-structured and easy to read
  • use a VCS (again, I recommend Git)
  • familiarize yourself with other parts of the stack (setup a Linux server and learn some basic networking skills, for a start)
  • design patterns

If you think you have the aptitude, you should definitely go for it!
